message.reasoning:
I need to decide whether to bid on Pacific Avenue in the current auction.

Pacific Avenue is the only remaining auction. The opponent has $263 cash. Mortgaging it would raise their funds to roughly $412. That is enough to pay the $300 Illinois rent without selling brown hotels. I will bid $2 and cap my offer at $149.

Neither player can complete the green set with Pacific Avenue. The main reason to block a cheap purchase is to prevent the opponent from mortgaging it for $150 and gaining a cash buffer against future rent payments.

I will bid $4, the minimum next bid. Dropping out is not an option.

Matching the opponent's bids one dollar at a time risks an endless auction. I should either bid aggressively to push them toward the $150 mortgage value or drop out.

Both players have an incentive to buy Pacific Avenue under $150. The opponent can mortgage it immediately for a net cash gain, while I can mortgage it later for cash and deny them the liquidity boost. The auction will likely end near the $150 break-even point.

Pacific Avenue is not worth paying more than $150. Its unimproved rent is only $26, and neither player can complete the green set without other properties. The real value is the mortgage arbitrage under $150 and blocking the opponent from that same profit.

A $149 win nets me $1 cash plus a mortgage. A $3 win gives the opponent $147 in liquidity. I am checking whether my two-house rent on Illinois Avenue covers that buffer.

Baltic Avenue hotel rent is $450. That is a major threat if the opponent lands there. My kill shots are Park Place hotel and Boardwalk four houses.

A Park Place hotel would collect $1500 in rent. Boardwalk with four houses pays $1700, and a hotel there would pay $2000. The opponent has hotels on Mediterranean and Baltic, so liquidating them to raise cash is complicated. Their total liquidation value is roughly $1143–$1193, which means a $1500 rent would bankrupt them.

Bidding $150 would tie the auction and prevent the opponent from gaining a cash buffer, but it would cost me $150 now. I still have enough cash to cover the Baltic hotel rent even after that loss. The real risk is overpaying if the opponent keeps bidding.

The opponent is clearly contesting the auction and understands the mortgage arbitrage. A jump bid to $50 or $100 would risk overpaying if they drop out. Since their maximum rational bid is likely $149, I should be willing to match that ceiling.

A jump bid to $149 would guarantee the property at the maximum rational price. If the opponent bids $150, they would overpay and lose the mortgage arbitrage. That is actually favorable for me.

If the opponent wins at a price of $113 or less, they can mortgage Pacific Avenue and still have enough cash to pay the $300 Illinois rent without selling their brown hotels. This confirms the $113 ceiling as the critical point where the auction becomes dangerous.

The $113 threshold is exact. If the opponent pays more than $113, mortgaging Pacific Avenue leaves them with less than $300, so they must sell buildings to pay the Illinois rent. If they pay more than $150, their cash after mortgage drops below their starting $263, making the purchase a net loss.

I am weighing whether to jump to $114 immediately. That would push the opponent out of the danger zone where they can pay the Illinois rent from mortgage cash. Bidding up to $149 is safer but slower.

Bidding $114 would net $36 profit if the opponent drops out, since I could mortgage the property for $150. If they continue bidding past that point, they enter a zone where mortgaging Pacific Avenue still cannot cover the $300 Illinois rent.

However, jumping to $114 is only worthwhile if the opponent will keep bidding until their maximum regardless of price. Otherwise, a slower incremental bid is preferable because it lets me win at a lower cost if they drop early.
